11056-trial-and-triumph:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote this rediscovered novel about Annette, a mischievous, hard-headed girl who torments her aunt Susan. Annette pours oil on a neighbour's clean steps, upsetting Mrs. Larkins, a proud housekeeper who believes beating is the only cure for bad children. Aunt Susan, mother of six, says all her children together never gave her as much trouble as Annette alone.

Later chapters follow Mr. Thomas, a young man building a business and opening gates to others, generous, conservative in good things, and open to new ideas that make life nobler. Harper links childhood trial to adult triumph, with lessons on discipline, kindness, and self-help. The novel gives readers an African American writer's domestic story, warm, moral, and rooted in community life.
1275-alexandria-and-her-schools-four-lec:
Charles Kingsley, the novelist and clergyman, gives four lectures on Alexandria, the Egyptian city where Greek learning met Jewish and Christian thought. He traces its schools from the Museum and its library through Philo, Clement, and the Neoplatonists, to the city's fall.

Kingsley writes with a Victorian's zeal for the meeting of faith and reason, and his lectures praise Alexandria as a crossroads of minds. The book is short and vivid, if dated in its judgments. It suits readers who like the history of ideas in lecture form. Kingsley's lectures give a vivid, short entry to Alexandria's schools.
2164-the-lumley-autograph:
Susan Fenimore Cooper, identified in Graham's Magazine as the author of Rural Hours, tells a short tale built around an autograph and the Lumley name. Published in 1851, the story turns on letters, reputation, and a scrap of handwriting. Cooper published the tale in Graham's Magazine in 1851, when magazine fiction was booming.

Cooper writes with the care of a daughter of James Fenimore Cooper, and the tale suits readers of mid-century magazine fiction. Its interest lies less in plot than in manners, memory, and the value placed on a famous name. The autograph plot turns on how a signature can carry fame, fraud, or simple human vanity.
22258-tales-of-the-caliph:
Hafiz Adam wrote Tales of the Caliph as new adventures of Haroun Alraschid, the caliph of the Arabian Nights. Haroun was in the habit, as everyone knows, of wandering Baghdad after nightfall in disguise. He went to see that justice was done, Adam admits, but also in hope of adventure. Many of his wanderings are already famous; these, the author promises, are no whit less interesting.

New tales follow the caliph and his vizier through markets, divans, and midnight streets. Justice, wit, and mercy resolve each night's puzzle. The book is an Edwardian imitation of the Arabian Nights, written by an Indian author for English readers. It keeps the old frame with a fresh stock of stories.
26861-the-temple-of-nature-or-the-origin:
Erasmus Darwin, author of The Botanic Garden, Zoonomia, and Phytologia, published this poem with philosophical notes in London in 1803. A preface dated from the Priory near Derby on January 1, 1802, disowns deep reasoning. The poem aims to amuse by bringing nature's operations before the imagination in the order time presented them. Its machinery comes from the Eleusinian mysteries, where a hierophant explained the philosophy of nature to initiates through allegoric scenery.

Canto one treats the production of life, beginning beneath the sea with spontaneous minute animals, irritation, appetency, and sensation. Vegetables and animals improve by reproduction, rocks of shell and coral rise, islands and continents lift by earthquake, and animals emigrate from the sea. The tadpole, the lizard, the beaver, and the whale mark stages of the ascent, and Venus rising from the sea stands as emblem of organic nature.
4347-my-young-alcides-a-faded-photograph:
Charlotte M. Yonge called this novel a faded photograph, and its subtitle points to its game: a modern Hercules in a shooting-coat. In her preface she admits the idea insisted on being worked out, even at the risk of travestying the Farnese statue in country dress. The Greek myth, she notes, also echoes Samson of old.

The chapters translate the labors into English life: the Arghouse inheritance, the lion of Neme Heath, the dragon's head, the capture in the snow, and the champion's belt. A strong young hero faces cattle stealers, a bloodhound, and golden fruit. Yonge turns myth into a domestic adventure, with morals as well as marvels.
5075-the-lion-of-the-north-a-tale-of-the:
G. A. Henty's Lion of the North opens late on a spring afternoon in 1630. Clouds mass over the hilltops of southern Scotland. Fierce wind drives rain before it. Three days of rain have turned every mountain burn into a boiling torrent. Rivers have flooded the low valleys. Evening closes in as a lad of sixteen gazes across the swollen Nith rushing past in turbid flood.

The invitation of the first chapter draws the boy toward Gustavus Adolphus and the Thirty Years' War, where a Scottish lad finds his fortune among Swedish armies. Henty's tale mixes history with adventure in his usual brisk style. Readers get a story of the Lion of the North's wars, seen through young Scottish eyes.
6444-the-boys-of-bellwood-school-or-fran:
Frank V. Webster follows Frank Jordan of Tipton in The Boys of Bellwood School, subtitled Frank Jordan's Triumph. A stickpin opens the trouble. Frank bought it at Mace's jewelry store with money he earned, but his aunt calls him extravagant. She says circumstances do not alter cases when a boy is a spendthrift. Frank lives with miserly, fault finding Miss Tabitha Brown while his invalid father seeks health in the South, his mother nursing him there.

For nearly a month the lad has not enjoyed life very greatly, and two thoughts fill his mind most. Later chapters promise a tinker boy, a diamond bracelet, Gill Mace, a ruined house, an astonishing clue, and a confidence man. A mid scene shows a farmer running a swindler down a railway car and tossing him toward a ditch by the depot. Webster writes schoolboy adventure with a hero earning his own way.
7356-the-boy-scout-camera-club-or-the-co:
Scout Master G. Harvey Ralphson's Boy Scout Camera Club, or The Confession of a Photograph, opens with Frank crying that a child's face looks down from above. Its chapters promise a lost foreign prince, a hole in the attic floor, a box's contents, a camp in the mountain, and signals in the canyon. A mint in the mountains, Uncle Ike, a lank mule as decoy, and Jack's elegant chicken pie follow. The black hand game, three days to move in, and a night on the summit complete the list.

The scouts' camera turns detective, as a photograph confesses what eyes missed. Ralphson writes brisk boys' adventure, mixing camp craft with mystery and humour. Young readers get scouting, sleuthing, and mountain fun in one lively tale.
749-barlaam-and-ioasaph:
A tale long ascribed to St. John of Damascus tells of Ioasaph, a prince shut away from sorrow, and Barlaam, the hermit who teaches him the Christian faith. The text was likely translated into Greek in the eleventh century from an older eastern source. It follows the prince as he meets age, sickness, and death for the first time and seeks the truth behind them.

Parables and debates carry the teaching, with stories inside the story that linger in the mind. The work blends Indian legend with Christian thought, and it travelled across Europe for centuries. It matters as a bridge between East and West, and as one of the most loved religious romances of the Middle Ages.
8443-the-mysteries-of-montreal-being-rec:
Charlotte Fuhrer, a physician with over thirty years of practice in Montreal, writes of things she has seen in that city. Told with the skill of a Dumas or a Collins, they might astonish and startle readers. Her Mysteries of Montreal gathers recollections of a female physician, cases and scenes from a long career, under the motto that truth is stranger than fiction.

The book belongs to the city-mysteries genre, but with a doctor's authority behind it: hospitals, homes, and streets seen from inside medicine. Readers get Victorian Montreal through a woman professional's eyes, a rare viewpoint for its time. The cases, told as stories, mix sensation with social observation.
979-heroes-of-the-telegraph:
J. Munro wrote these lives of the heroes of the telegraph, men who wired the world. Munro, author of Electricity and Its Uses and Pioneers of Electricity, tells how Morse, Wheatstone, and their peers turned sparks into messages, and how cables crossed seas and continents.

Munro writes with a popular, admiring tone, mixing biography with clear accounts of circuits, keys, and codes. His heroes are workers as much as geniuses, and their triumphs came through trial and error. The book is a vivid record of the Victorian communications revolution, for readers who like science told through lives.
alexandria-and-her-schools-four-lectures:
Charles Kingsley delivered these four lectures at the Philosophical Institution in Edinburgh, and the text here follows the 1902 Macmillan printing of his historical lectures. His subject is Alexandria in Egypt, the great seat of learning in the ancient world. Kingsley admits in his preface that the subject was chosen for him and that the lectures are rough.

He traces the city's museum and library, its Greek philosophers, its Jewish scholars, and its early Christian teachers, who tried to wed faith to Greek thought. Figures such as Philo, Origen, and Hypatia pass through the account. The lectures show a Victorian clergyman reading ancient learning with warmth and strong opinions.
barlaam-and-ioasaph:
Barlaam and Ioasaph retells, in Christian dress, the legend of a prince who renounces his throne for the religious life. The hermit Barlaam secretly instructs the Indian prince Ioasaph, sheltered by his father from all knowledge of suffering, and converts him through parables. The 1914 Harvard edition, translated by G R Woodward and H Mattingly, supplies this text.

Tradition ascribes the work to Saint John of Damascus, though scholars believe the Greek version came from a Georgian original around the eleventh century. Behind it stands the life of the Buddha, carried west and baptized. Ioasaph's debates on God, righteousness, and the making of all things fill the middle chapters. Few medieval tales traveled farther.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aistulph:
Aistulph, King of the Lombards, died in 756, succeeding his brother Ratchis in 749 and setting about conquering all Italy. After taking Ravenna's Exarchate from the Greeks he was about to seize St. Peter's Patrimony. Pope Stephen II appealed to Frankish King Pepin the Short for aid.

Pepin led an army through the Alps, beating Aistulph and besieging him in Pavia in 754. Peace followed, with Aistulph surrendering the Exarchate and all conquered territory. Hardly had Pepin returned home when Aistulph besieged Rome and wasted the surrounding territory. Pepin again besieged Pavia, overpowered him, and exacted an indemnity and Comacchio. Pepin then endowed the Holy See with the rescued territories, Fulrad laying keys and deed on St. Peter's altar. A fall from his horse while hunting ended his life before he could renew war. He left no male issue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Saint Asaph was founded by Saint Kentigern about the mid-sixth century, in exile from his Scottish see. He built a monastery, Llanelwy, where the Clwyd and Elwy meet in North Wales. When he returned to Scotland in 573, Asaph, or Asa, succeeded him and was consecrated Bishop of Llanelwy.

At first the diocese matched the principality of Powys. It lost ground first to the Mercian advance marked by Watt's dyke, then to Offa's dyke after 798. Domesday Book gives scanty notes on a few churches and says nothing of the cathedral. Norman influence arrived in the twelfth century, when Archbishop Theobald consecrated Gilbert as bishop in 1143. Successors struggled, and Godfrey was driven off by poverty and Welsh hostility. By the mid-thirteenth century the diocese counted eight rural deaneries, seventy-nine churches, and nineteen chapels. By 1291 the deaneries had doubled. Cistercian houses stood at four sites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ange-de-saint:
Ange de Saint Joseph, French missionary friar of the Discalced Carmelites, was born at Toulouse in 1636 and died at Perpignan in 1697. His name was de la Brosse. In 1662 he took up Arabic at San Pancrazio in Rome, under Celestino a San Liduvina, brother of the Orientalist Golius. In 1664 he was sent East, learning Persian at Smyrna and Ispahan from Balthazar, a Carmelite.

He passed ten years in Persia and Arabia, as prior at Ispahan and at Basrah. When the Turks captured Basrah, he went to Constantinople and won the Sultan's protection through the French ambassador. Recalled to Rome in 1679, he became superior of missions in Holland, England, and Ireland in 1680. He was Provincial of his order at his death. His works include a Persian pharmacopoeia in Latin, published in 1681. His Gazophylacium linguae Persarum, a grammar with a dictionary in Latin, Italian, French, was published at Amsterdam in 1684.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-hermann-jo:
Blessed Hermann Joseph, a Premonstratensian monk and mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cologne about 1150 to parents once rich and now poor, he died at Hoven in 1241. Schooled from age seven, he showed a tender devotion to the Virgin Mary that lasted his whole life.

At St. Mary on the Capitol he knelt in childlike prayer, once offering an apple saved from his scanty meal to the Christ Child in Mary's arms. Entering Steinfeld abbey, he lived as a devout monk and mystic, famed for visions and for the name Joseph added to his own. The entry presents a saint of simple, lifelong devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-schrau:
Johann Schraudolph was a German historical painter best known for the frescoes of Speyer Cathedral. Born in the Allgau in 1808, he trained under Heinrich Hess, painting scenes from the life of St. Boniface in the Munich basilica and devotional pictures that won wide popularity, among them the Virgin with the Child Jesus and Christ as the Friend of Children.

On Hess's recommendation, King Louis I gave him the Speyer commission, the great work of his life. After fresh study in Rome, Schraudolph kept strict control of his assistants. He designed the cupola, choir, and nave compositions himself. He painted the hardest pictures with his own hand. The whole series sets out the divine plan of salvation. It gives special honor to the Virgin and the cathedral's patron saints. Its style won praise for correctness, harmony, and devotion rather than force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph:
Joseph was the eleventh son of Jacob, Rachel's firstborn, and ancestor of the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim. His story, told in Genesis 37 and 39 to 50, begins with his father's gift of a coat of many colors and his dreams of greatness, which stirred his brothers' hatred. At Dothan they sold him to traders bound for Egypt.

In Egypt Joseph rose from slavery and prison to power by interpreting dreams, including Pharaoh's dreams of famine. As the king's minister he stored grain, saved the land, and was at last reconciled with the brothers who had sold him. The entry also weighs the text's sources and the question of which Pharaoh ruled in Joseph's day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pandulph:
Pandulph was a papal legate and Bishop of Norwich who died at Rome on 16 September 1226. He is commonly but wrongly called Cardinal Pandulph, through confusion with Cardinal Pandulph Masca of Pisa, made cardinal in 1182 and dead in 1201. The mix-up would make the legate live over a hundred years past his ordination as subdeacon.

A Roman by birth, Pandulph served as clerk at Innocent III's court. Sent to England in 1211 to win King John's acceptance of Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury, he met only threats at Northampton. Sent again in 1213, he took part in the Dover Castle scene of 15 May. There John gave his crown to Pandulph and got it back as a papal fief. The king also paid 8,000 pounds as an instalment of tribute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-fitzr:
This entry follows Richard Fitzralph, a fourteenth-century scholar who became Archbishop of Armagh. Born at Dundalk around 1295, he studied and taught at Oxford, served as its chancellor, and held a string of church posts before his consecration at Armagh in 1346. He sent his priests to Oxford for deeper study, toured his province, and worked to improve both its money matters and its spiritual life.

Scholarship and controversy ran together through his career. He defended Armagh's claim to primacy against Dublin, acted at times as a peacemaker between English and Irish, and preached widely. At Avignon he pressed complaints by the English clergy against the mendicant friars, a dispute he carried into his treatise De Pauperie Salvatoris on poverty, ownership, and grace. Cited back to Avignon in 1357, he died there in 1360 with the quarrel still unresolved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-sa:
The Sisters of Saint Joseph began at Le Puy in Velay, France, founded by the Jesuit Jean-Paul Médaille. On 15 October 1650 he addressed the first sisters as a religious community, placed them under the protection of Saint Joseph, and gave them rules. Their work was the Christian education of children, and their dress was a black habit and veil with a white linen band and coif.

From Le Puy the congregation spread into many independent diocesan branches across France, America, and beyond. Sisters in Erie, Fall River, Philadelphia, and other dioceses ran parish schools, academies, orphanages, hospitals, and homes for the aged. The Erie branch alone counted 210 members in charge of 14 parish schools with 3,900 children, while Fall River counted 43 sisters in four schools. Branches also reached Australia and New Zealand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-asaph:
St. Asaph, or Asa, was the first bishop of the Welsh see of that name, in the second half of the sixth century. This entry admits that no Welsh life of him survives. Local tradition still points out his ash tree, church, well, and valley in Tengenel near Holywell, suggesting he once had a hermitage there. Jocelyn of Furness's life of St. Kentigern, or Mungo, founder of the Glasgow diocese, partly makes up for that lack.

During his exile about 545, Kentigern came to Wales. There he set up the Celtic monastery of Llanelwy, the church on the Elwy — the name the Welsh still give the town of St. Asaph. Of few Celtic monasteries do we know so much about building and government as about Llanelwy. Its church was built of smoothed wood, after the fashion of the Britons, since they could not yet build in stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-botulph:
St. Botulph, or Botolph, was abbot, date of birth unknown, dead about 680. This entry follows the saint whose name lives on in the American city of Boston, Massachusetts. He was certainly a historical personage, though the story of his life is very confused and unsatisfactory. What we know of him comes mainly from Folcard's short biography — Folcard was a monk of St. Bertin and abbot of Thorney, writing in the eleventh century.

According to Folcard, Botulph's parents were noble Saxons and Christians, and he was sent with his brother Adulph to the Continent for study. Adulph remained abroad, where he is said to have become bishop of Utrecht, though his name occurs in no ancient list. Returning to England, Botulph won the favour of a certain Ethelmund, king of the southern Angles, whose sisters were known to him from Germany. Ethelmund permitted him to choose a site for his monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joseph:
Joseph, spouse of Mary and foster-father of Jesus, is known reliably only from the Gospels' first chapters. Matthew and Luke supply the chief, practically the only reliable, sources for his life. Apocryphal literature, by contrast, is full of details on points canonical writings leave untouched. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 warns that exclusion from the canon casts strong suspicion on those contents.

Among apocryphal works touching Joseph are the Gospel of James, Pseudo-Matthew, the Gospel of Mary's Nativity, the Story of Joseph the Carpenter, and the Life of Joseph. Even granting some recorded facts may rest on trustworthy traditions, the entry says, it is mostly impossible to sift true history's particles from surrounding fancies. The article therefore builds on Matthew and Luke, treating apocrypha as suspect abundance, not as biography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-rolph:
Thomas Rolph, a surgeon born in 1800, wrote on emigration and took a lively part in Catholic affairs. A younger son of Dr. Thomas Rolph, he practised at Crutched Friars in London, where a clash with the Anglican rector over tithes led him to petition the Commons and publish pamphlets on the subject. He also wrote against the Religious Tract Society and against phrenology.

In 1832 he sailed to the West Indies, the United States and Canada, where his brother John led the Upper Canada assembly's committee. Settling for a time in Canada as a government emigration agent, he returned to England in 1839 and published guides for settlers, including the Emigrants' Manual of 1843. He died of apoplexy at Portsmouth in February 1858.
doe-osti-3017683-bioreactor-optimization: Bioreactors got multi-phase-optimized, and this DOE CRADA final models the flow. The pages detail the report findings. The bio folks get their closeout. The models were multi-phase. The closeout was bio. The flow was models. The optimization was bioreactor.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurtonJoseph_Bu:
Jack Anderson, the syndicated columnist whose Washington Merry-Go-Round reached millions, built this column on secret Senate testimony. The testimony, given behind closed doors, said that the CIA and FBI had plotted to murder enemy agents.

Anderson reports evidence of exotic assassination weapons and of training sites in the southeastern United States. Columns like this one carried the Church Committee era's revelations to newspaper readers who would never open a Senate report. The piece is muckraking journalism in its classic form: leaked testimony, official secrecy, and a columnist willing to print what he had been told.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MazzarellaJosep:
United Press International reported from Cleveland on January 9 about a lawsuit in federal court. Patrolman Joseph Mazzarella was suing Secret Service agent Rufus Youngblood for 50,000 dollars in damages. Mazzarella said he was hurt by an open car door during President Johnson's 1964 visit. The article covers testimony in the case.

Youngblood was famous for shielding Johnson in Dallas on the day Kennedy was killed. A suit over a car door, brought by an injured patrolman, belongs to the ordinary legal wake of presidential travel. The wire story records the claim, the amount, and the courtroom testimony, a small civil case hanging on a famous name.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ThompsonJoseph_: An FBI memorandum dated January 28, 1964, concerns Joseph Thompson, a member of the U.S. Air Force Reserve. It notes his ties to the Civil Air Patrol, the same youth organization Lee Harvey Oswald had joined in New Orleans. Two months after the assassination, agents were still mapping Oswald's old connections. The memo is one small result of that work, kept in the bureau's files.
heroes-of-the-telegraph:
John Munro wrote Heroes of the Telegraph as a sequel to his Pioneers of Electricity, telling the lives of the men who introduced the electric telegraph. His contents honor Charles Wheatstone, Samuel Morse, William Thomson, and William Siemens in full chapters. Philipp Reis, Graham Bell, Thomas Edison, and David Hughes follow, with Gauss, Weber, Cooke, and Elisha Gray in an appendix.

Munro explains each invention alongside its maker's life, from the origin of the telegraph to submarine cables grappled up from sandy shore ends. The tone is Victorian admiration, but the technical detail is real. Readers get both a history of electrical communication and a portrait gallery of the nineteenth century's inventing heroes, rivals included.
my-young-alcides-a-faded-photograph:
Charlotte M. Yonge shapes this tale on the myth of Hercules. Her preface says the old myth pressed her to work it out. She feared dressing the Farnese statue in a shooting coat. Still, the notion grew too deep and strong to drop.

Yonge reads Hercules as a figure of the true Victor. His great crime made his life a bondage of atonement. The choice of Virtue over Vice stands at his path's start. Slain passions rise again like the many-headed sin. She calls her hero a faded photograph of that pattern, a man who conquers himself by repentance and toil.
nasa-tm-19660012926-analytic-representat:
James C G Walker, at the Institute for Space Studies in New York, recast a well-known set of atmosphere models into formula form. Jacchia had published static diffusion models in 1964 to match satellite drag data. Drag reveals air density, because thin air slows a satellite bit by bit. Walker's work modifies the mathematical method behind those models, the catalog note says.

A formula that gives density directly is faster to use than tables. Orbit computers of the era needed that speed. Representing the models in analytic form let many users share one result. Walker's paper sits between observation and practice: satellite drag above, and a usable equation for everyone who predicts orbits below.
the-boy-scout-camera-club-or-the-confess: Scout Master G. Harvey Ralphson wrote The Boy Scout Camera Club, or The Confession of a Photograph. The chapter list starts with a lost foreign prince and a hole in an attic floor. What the Box Contained and A Camp in the Mountain come next. Signals in a canyon, a mint in the mountains, and Uncle Ike come next. A black hand game and The Call of the Pack close the heads shown.
the-boys-of-bellwood-school-or-frank-jor: Frank V. Webster wrote The Boys of Bellwood School, or Frank Jordan's Triumph. The parts start at Frank Jordan's home, then bring in a tinker boy and a diamond bracelet. Gill Mace, a ruined house, and a startling clue come next. A confidence man, a boy guardian, and a stubborn rebel crowd the mid parts. Late parts put Frank in prison and under arrest, then clean up the mess. The tale itself opens with a sharp query to Frank about a stickpin, and no more of it is shown.
the-lion-of-the-north-a-tale-of-the-time:
G. A. Henty opens his tale of Gustavus Adolphus times with a preface to young readers, in pages matching the other record of this title held here. Boys loaded with school learning, he says, rarely study foreign history, though the Thirty Years War shaped modern Europe. That war grew from an imperial drive to crush German Protestantism.

Henty reports that Germany lost nearly a third of her people, with whole towns and villages wiped out in some states. His story takes the war first part, from Sweden entry under her chivalrous king to the deaths of Gustavus and Wallenstein. A Scottish boy soldier carries readers through the campaigns.
the-lumley-autograph:
Susan Fenimore Cooper wrote The Lumley Autograph, published in Graham's Magazine in 1851, though a transcriber's introduction notes she wrote it as early as 1845. Her father, James Fenimore Cooper, first offered it to Graham's himself, asking at least twenty-five dollars. The story grew, the introduction explains, from the constant stream of letters her father received. They begged for his autograph, pages of his manuscripts, or autographs of other famous men who had written to him. The introduction praises the tale's double edge.

Its broad satire targets the autograph-collecting mania of the mid-nineteenth century. Beneath that runs a sharper irony: a poet's frantic appeal for help becomes a plaything of the rich, while the poet who wrote it died in want. Cooper generally answered the autograph hunters courteously, and after his death Susan kept answering them.
the-mysteries-of-montreal-being-recollec:
Charlotte Fuhrer's The Mysteries of Montreal, subtitled Recollections of a Female Physician, opens with an introduction dated Montreal, May 1881. Fuhrer practiced medicine in the city for over thirty years. While waiting at night for babies to arrive, she beguiled the hours by telling patients stories from her own experience, and their startled faces taught her the tales had power.

Enquiries about publication led her to print the volume, changing only names of persons and places to prevent identification. Readers who knew the parties would recognise them under false names, she warns. Chapter I turns to her early life. Her father, an officer in the Hanoverian Army, died while she was a child. At seventeen she became a governess in Hamburg, where she met her husband, Gustav Schroeder.
trial-and-triumph:
Frances E. W. Harper's Trial and Triumph, edited by Frances Smith Foster, presents itself as a rediscovered novel. A transcriber's note sketches Harper's life: born free at Baltimore in 1825, orphaned at three, and raised by an uncle who taught and fought for civil rights. She became a lecturer, suffragist, poet, and novelist across sixty years.

Chapter one opens in a household worn down by young Annette's mischief. Aunt Susan counts six children who together caused less trouble than this one girl. Annette has poured oil on a neighbor's clean steps, and Mrs. Larkins is in an uproar next door. The scene sets a spirited heroine against the adults who despair of her.
